instruction:
I'm doing a piece of coursework and need an illustration for a science-communication article on industrial automation — the whole indoor scene of an industrial packaging line in a cleanroom. The reference photo is attached; please stay close to the room structure and equipment layout in the image, don't re-plan it — it's going to be used as a figure with callouts, so the structure has to be accurate.

The space is a rectangular cleanroom: light/white flat walls, bright and open, a suspended ceiling with a regular grid of recessed light panels, a light-colored anti-static floor with clean seams, and an otherwise plain, cleanroom-style finish. Estimate the bay and depth from the image proportions.

The hero of the shot is the stainless-steel packaging machine running along the depth of the room. A light-colored conveyor belt runs through it, with evenly spaced products/trays waiting to be packed. Above the machine, an adjustable articulated arm holds a large touchscreen / HMI panel facing the operator. Build the mechanical guts properly — pneumatic cylinders, actuators, linkages, guide rails, metal-profile framing, with believable fits and repeated arrays — and wrap the whole thing in a transparent guard enclosure with stainless frames, plus a few small nameplates as accents (text needn't be legible). Also drop in two staff in white lab coats and hairnets, one operating the touchscreen in the foreground and one in the background — just placeholders for scale, not a modeling focus.

Two things matter most: the image should read clean so I can add labels and leader lines later, and the structure should be accurate, not invented. Estimate part sizes from common industrial specs and the image; no need for millimeters — use your judgment on detail.

Materials, light color temperature and that slight teal cast, camera position and render settings are all in the attached `scene_spec.md` — follow that. Mood-wise just match the original: cool with a subtle teal/green tint, that cleanroom feel.

Give me a high-res render, and keep the Blender file — I may want to change the camera or angle afterwards.
